| **Validation should generally occur before first use, with enhanced controls if a model is used before validation.** SR 11-7 states validation generally occurs prior to first use, and if urgent use occurs before validation, limitations should be communicated and use limits or closer monitoring should be imposed. (SR 11-7 §V, “Model Validation and Monitoring”) | The SOP requires annual validation and states that MLflow production promotion requires MRM validation sign-off, and annual recalibration must be validated before Q1 regulatory capital calculation. (SOP-FIN-010 §§6.2 Ctl-010, Ctl-060; §6.3 MLflow Model Registry access controls) | **Partial.** The SOP has some pre-production controls, but it should explicitly prohibit first use of any new or materially changed regulatory capital model before independent validation, unless a documented temporary-use exception includes limitations, compensating controls, enhanced monitoring, and senior approval. |
| **Ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis must assess continued reliability and fitness for purpose.** SR 11-7 expects ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis to detect deterioration and support decisions on adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment. (SR 11-7 §V, “Model Validation and Monitoring”) | The SOP requires quarterly model performance monitoring, including PD back-testing, LGD outcome comparison, AUROC/AR, PSI, Hosmer-Lemeshow testing, K-S statistics, threshold breaches, root-cause analysis, capital impact quantification, and fit-for-purpose assessment. (SOP-FIN-010 §§4.2 RC-P-004–RC-P-005, 5.10, 6.2 Ctl-030–Ctl-038, 6.4) | **Compliant.** This is one of the SOP’s strongest areas. |
| **Effective challenge must be performed by objective, expert, sufficiently independent personnel with authority to effect change.** SR 11-7 describes effective challenge as critical analysis by objective experts with expertise, independence, standing, and influence. (SR 11-7 §III/§IV discussion of effective challenge; §VI “Governance and Controls”) | The SOP separates MRM from model development, prohibits validators from having developed the same models within the prior 36 months, assigns MRM accountability for validation, gives the CRO and Head of MRM challenge roles, and requires Model Risk Committee review. (SOP-FIN-010 §§3.1–3.3, 5.5–5.6, 5.10, 6.1–6.2) | **Compliant.** The independence, challenge, and committee structures are well defined. |
| **Governance should include clear roles, responsibilities, controls, and accountability across the model lifecycle.** SR 11-7 states governance should be supported by clear policies, effective controls, and accountability for development, validation, and ongoing monitoring. (SR 11-7 §VI, “Governance and Controls”) | The SOP includes a RACI, named accountable owners, three lines of defense, control catalogue, management attestation, issue escalation, exception governance, internal audit review, and Board/committee escalation. (SOP-FIN-010 §§3, 4, 6, 7.4, 8) | **Compliant.** The governance framework is mature and well aligned to SR 11-7. |
| **Documentation and model inventory should support continuity, remediation, exceptions, and aggregate model risk management.** SR 11-7 states effective model inventories contain sufficient information to understand model risks individually and in aggregate, and documentation supports continuity, tracking recommendations, responses, exceptions, and remediation. (SR 11-7 §VI, “Governance and Controls” — Model Inventory and Documentation) | The SOP requires model inventory records, technical reference documents, code repositories, data lineage, model limitation disclosures, validation reports, findings tracking, and exception registers. (SOP-FIN-010 §§4.2 RC-P-003, 6.2 Ctl-020–Ctl-025, 8.3) | **Mostly compliant.** Inventory and documentation controls are strong, but the SOP should add a defined aggregate model risk assessment for common data, assumptions, overlays, methodologies, and dependencies across PD, LGD, EAD, macro, and RWA calculation models. |
| **Third-party/vendor models and products remain subject to model risk management.** SR 11-7 states vendor products must be validated and monitored, including understanding conceptual soundness, design, development data, performance, customization, overlays, and adjustments. (SR 11-7 §VII, “Vendor and Other Third-Party Products”) | The SOP identifies SAS as the regulatory capital engine provider and KPMG as external validation firm, and it includes independent replication of model outputs and external validation of A-IRB models. (SOP-FIN-010 §§1.3, 5.5, 6.2 Ctl-012) | **Partial/gap.** The SOP does not sufficiently describe vendor-model due diligence or validation of proprietary/vendor components of the SAS Regulatory Capital Engine, including vendor methodology review, limitations, release/change review, SOC/vendor assurance review, or ongoing vendor performance monitoring. |
| **Model overlays, adjustments, and overrides should be supported by analysis and controls.** SR 11-7 notes outcome analysis can support overlays or adjustments, and model users should understand and communicate limitations. (SR 11-7 §V, “Model Validation and Monitoring”; §VII for vendor/customized adjustments) | The SOP requires every overlay or override to be documented with rationale, date, approving authority, sunset date, and capital impact; it also requires quarterly Model Risk Committee reporting and a cumulative CET1 impact threshold. (SOP-FIN-010 §§4.2 RC-P-007, 5.6, 6.2 Ctl-050–Ctl-052) | **Compliant.** Override governance is strong. |
| **Internal audit should assess whether model risk management practices are rigorous and policies are implemented, rather than duplicating model validation.** SR 11-7 states internal audit generally evaluates the rigor and effectiveness of model risk management practices and policy implementation. (SR 11-7 §VI, “Governance and Controls”) | The SOP assigns Internal Audit an annual independent review of the regulatory capital reporting control environment, including design and operating effectiveness of controls and sample testing of submissions. (SOP-FIN-010 §§6.1, 7.4) | **Compliant.** Internal audit’s role is appropriately framed as independent assurance. |

## Key gaps to remediate

1. **Add explicit pre-use and material-change validation gates.**  
   SR 11-7 expects validation generally before first use and enhanced controls where pre-use validation is not complete. (SR 11-7 §V, “Model Validation and Monitoring”) SOP-FIN-010 should state that no new or materially changed PD, LGD, EAD, macro, RWA, or vendor capital model component may be used in production regulatory capital reporting without documented MRM validation approval, except under a tightly controlled exception. (SOP-FIN-010 §§6.2, 8)

2. **Strengthen vendor-product model risk management for SAS and other third-party components.**  
   SR 11-7 applies model risk management principles to vendor products and expects understanding of conceptual soundness, design, development data, performance, customization, and overlays. (SR 11-7 §VII, “Vendor and Other Third-Party Products”) SOP-FIN-010 should add a vendor model risk section covering SAS release validation, vendor methodology documentation, change-impact assessment, user acceptance testing, SOC/vendor assurance review, limitations, and monitoring. (SOP-FIN-010 §§1.3, 5.5, 6.3)

3. **Define aggregate model risk assessment.**  
   SR 11-7 expects model risk to be assessed individually and in aggregate, including dependencies from common assumptions, data, methodologies, and interactions among models. (SR 11-7 §III/§IV model risk discussion; §VI “Governance and Controls”) SOP-FIN-010 should require at least annual aggregate review across PD, LGD, EAD, macroeconomic overlay, RWA engine, data pipelines, and supervisory floors. (SOP-FIN-010 §§6.2, 7.2)

4. **Make benchmarking operationally explicit.**  
   SR 11-7 identifies benchmarking and outcome analysis as practical validation/monitoring tools, depending on model type and use. (SR 11-7 §V, “Components of Model Validation — Conceptual Soundness/Outcomes Analysis”) SOP-FIN-010’s policy says monitoring includes benchmarking, but the detailed QMPMR procedure does not clearly specify alternative-model or external benchmark tests beyond supervisory-floor comparison. (SOP-FIN-010 §§4.2 RC-P-004, 5.10)

## Conclusion

SOP-FIN-010 is **well designed and largely aligned** with SR 11-7’s model risk management expectations for regulatory capital models, especially for independent validation, ongoing monitoring, governance, documentation, issue escalation, management attestation, and overrides. However, it should not be rated fully compliant until it adds more explicit controls for **pre-use validation, vendor-model oversight, aggregate model risk, and benchmarking implementation**.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Is SOP-CLIN-006 (Clinical AI Human Override Procedures) compliant with HIPAA's expectations for ePHI access control and audit when clinicians override AI outputs?
question.expected_answer: Compliant. The SOP implements role-based access control to ePHI (§164.312(a)) for the clinician override interface, automatic audit logging of every override event including user, timestamp, reason code, and PHI accessed (§164.312(b) audit controls), and integrity controls (§164.312(c)) so that override actions cannot alter the underlying ePHI record. The override procedure preserves the minimum-necessary standard (§164.502(b)) and ties into the workforce-training programme (§164.308(a)(5)). PHI accessed via override pathways is included in accounting-of-disclosures procedures where required.

output.answer:
SOP-CLIN-006 is **partially compliant** with HIPAA Security Rule expectations for ePHI access control and audit controls during clinician override of AI outputs. It has strong override-event logging and role-based access controls, but it does not fully document all required HIPAA access-control elements—most notably an **emergency access procedure**—and it could better specify access-rights lifecycle review and audit-log examination procedures.

| HIPAA expectation | HIPAA citation | SOP-CLIN-006 evidence | Assessment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Limit access to ePHI systems to authorized persons or software programs | 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(1); access rights tied to § 164.308(a)(4) | SOP § 6.1 limits Accept/Modify/Reject to users with the `ClarityClinicalUser` role; read-only users do not see override buttons; role assignment is managed through IAM integrated with customer AD/LDAP via SAML 2.0. | **Mostly compliant** |
| Unique user identification | 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(2)(i) | SOP § 6.2 maps “Unique User Identification” to unique user IDs via LDAP/SAML; override logs include User ID. | **Compliant** |
| Person or entity authentication | 45 CFR § 164.312(d) | SOP § 6.1 requires MFA for production sessions; SOP § 5.2 assumes clinician authentication via host EHR SSO and active patient context; SOP § 6.2 maps MFA and unique user IDs to person/entity authentication. | **Compliant** |
| Emergency access procedure | 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(2)(ii) | SOP § 8.1 addresses platform unavailability and manual EHR documentation, but it does **not** establish a procedure for obtaining necessary ePHI during an emergency. | **Gap** |
| Automatic logoff, if reasonable and appropriate | 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(2)(iii); addressable under § 164.306(d)(3) | SOP § 6.2 states automatic logoff occurs after 15 minutes of inactivity. | **Compliant** |
| Encryption/decryption of ePHI, if reasonable and appropriate | 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(2)(iv); addressable under § 164.306(d)(3) | SOP § 6.2 maps encryption and transmission protection: TLS 1.3 in transit, HTTPS for PHI in rationale text, and cryptographic controls for audit tables. | **Compliant** |
| Audit controls that record and examine activity in systems containing or using ePHI | 45 CFR § 164.312(b) | SOP § 6.2 logs override dialog opening, Modify, Reject, Explicit Accept, Tacit Accept, and post-hoc rationale edits with timestamp, user ID, patient ID, session ID, action, model/recommendation IDs, pre/post states, rationale, and success/failure. SOP § 3.1 assigns monthly audit-trail integrity verification to the Product Team with CCO accountability. | **Mostly compliant** |
| Integrity protections against improper alteration or destruction of ePHI | 45 CFR § 164.312(c)(1) | SOP § 6.1 states override audit records are cryptographically signed, immutable, and correction is by supplemental note rather than altering the original; SOP § 6.2 maps integrity controls to cryptographic signing and message authentication codes. | **Compliant** |
| Written policies/procedures and retention of required documentation for 6 years | 45 CFR § 164.316(a), § 164.316(b)(1), § 164.316(b)(2)(i) | SOP § 6.2 states audit records are retained for at least 6 years; SOP § 11 has revision history; SOP § 10 lists related policies. | **Compliant for the SOP/audit records described** |
| Policies for authorizing, establishing, documenting, reviewing, and modifying access rights | 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(4)(i), § 164.308(a)(4)(ii)(B)-(C) | SOP § 6.1 describes RBAC and IAM/AD/LDAP provisioning, but it does not define review frequency, deprovisioning triggers, privileged-access review, or how access changes are documented for clinician override privileges. | **Partial / needs detail** |
| Security awareness and training | 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(5)(i) | SOP § 9 requires initial and annual Clinical AI Human Oversight Training and retains records for 6 years; however, the listed curriculum is AI/override-focused rather than clearly HIPAA security-awareness-focused. | **Partial for HIPAA security training; strong for clinical override training** |

### Key compliance strengths

1. **Access is role-gated and authenticated.** The SOP limits override actions to authenticated users with the `ClarityClinicalUser` role, aligning with HIPAA’s access-control requirement to allow access only to persons or software programs with granted access rights. See 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(1) and SOP § 6.1.

2. **Override activity is highly auditable.** The SOP logs clinician identity, patient ID, timestamp, session ID, action, model/recommendation IDs, rationale, pre/post states, and outcome success/failure for override events. This supports HIPAA’s audit-controls requirement to record and examine activity in systems that contain or use ePHI. See 45 CFR § 164.312(b) and SOP § 6.2.

3. **Audit-trail integrity is well addressed.** Immutable logs, cryptographic signatures, no deletion API, and correction-by-supplemental-note align with HIPAA’s integrity requirement to protect ePHI from improper alteration or destruction. See 45 CFR § 164.312(c)(1) and SOP §§ 6.1–6.2.

4. **Retention is aligned.** HIPAA requires Security Rule documentation to be retained for 6 years, and the SOP states override audit records are retained for at least 6 years. See 45 CFR § 164.316(b)(2)(i) and SOP § 6.2.

### Required remediation items

1. **Add an explicit emergency access procedure.** HIPAA requires an emergency access procedure as a required implementation specification under access control. See 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(2)(ii). SOP § 8.1 addresses system failure and manual documentation, but it does not define how authorized workforce members obtain necessary ePHI access during an emergency.

2. **Document access lifecycle controls.** HIPAA expects policies for access authorization and access establishment/modification. See 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(4)(ii)(B)-(C). SOP § 6.1 should be expanded to specify provisioning approval, periodic access review, deprovisioning upon role change/termination, emergency role handling, and documentation of access-right changes.

3. **Clarify audit-log examination, not just logging.** HIPAA audit controls require mechanisms that “record and examine” system activity. See 45 CFR § 164.312(b). SOP § 6.2 records sufficient detail, and SOP § 3.1 references monthly audit-trail integrity verification, but the SOP should more clearly define who reviews override audit logs for inappropriate access, what exception reports are run, review cadence, escalation thresholds, and evidence retention.

4. **Tie training more explicitly to HIPAA security.** HIPAA requires a security awareness and training program for workforce members. See 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(5)(i). SOP § 9 is strong for AI override competency, but it should either incorporate or cross-reference HIPAA security training for users who access ePHI through override workflows.

### Bottom line

SOP-CLIN-006 is well designed for **clinician override logging, non-repudiation, rationale capture, and role-gated override access**, and it substantially supports HIPAA’s technical safeguards for access control, audit controls, integrity, authentication, and transmission security. However, it is not fully compliant as written because it lacks a required HIPAA emergency access procedure and does not sufficiently specify access-right lifecycle management and audit-log examination procedures.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Does SOP-AIML-007 (Model Retraining and Continuous Learning) align with NIST AI RMF's MEASURE and MANAGE functions for handling distributional drift and emergent risks?
question.expected_answer: Compliant. SOP-AIML-007 implements continuous monitoring of distributional drift, performance decay, and fairness/bias metrics with defined thresholds (MEASURE 2/3/4), tied to retraining triggers and approval gates (MANAGE 1/2/3). Retraining requires re-validation against pre-defined acceptance criteria, documented retraining-data provenance, and re-issuance of model cards. Stakeholder feedback channels (clinical/business teams) close the loop into MAP for emergent-risk identification. Risk tolerances from GOVERN are referenced for prioritisation.
question.notes: Positive case; NIST AI RMF boost.

output.answer:
Yes — **SOP-AIML-007 substantially aligns with NIST AI RMF 1.0 MEASURE and MANAGE for distributional drift**, but it is **only partially aligned for emergent risks** because it lacks a clearly defined mechanism for incorporating end-user/affected-community feedback, appeals, and external risk intelligence into ongoing risk measurement and response.

| Area | NIST AI RMF expectation | SOP-AIML-007 evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Distributional drift measurement** | NIST expects organizations to select and apply appropriate AI risk metrics, and to reassess metrics and controls regularly. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 1.1–1.2**) | SOP defines automated drift metrics and thresholds: PSI > 0.25, KS p < 0.01, KL divergence > 0.15, label drift, and concept-drift proxies using AUC/PR-AUC degradation. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.1.2**) | **Aligned.** The SOP uses concrete, quantitative drift metrics and rolling windows. |
| **Production monitoring** | NIST requires AI system functionality and behavior to be monitored in production. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 2.4**) | SOP requires continuous production inference-log monitoring through Meridian Drift Monitor and operational dashboards refreshing as often as 5 minutes. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.1.2**, **§7.2**) | **Aligned.** Monitoring is continuous and operationalized. |
| **Tracking risks over time, including emergent risks** | NIST calls for approaches, personnel, and documentation to regularly identify and track existing, unanticipated, and emergent AI risks based on intended and actual performance in deployed contexts. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 3.1**) | SOP tracks drift events, performance degradation, fairness trends, rollback rate, MTTR/MTTD, audit findings, adverse-event triggers, and RCA status. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.1.2–§5.1.4**, **§5.7**, **§7.1–§7.3**) | **Mostly aligned.** It covers performance-based and incident-driven emergent risks, but not broader stakeholder-reported or societal/contextual emergent risks. |
| **Validation under deployment-like conditions** | NIST requires performance or assurance criteria to be measured and documented for conditions similar to deployment settings. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 2.3**) | SOP requires temporal holdout testing, shadow deployment for Tier 1 and Tier 2 models, side-by-side candidate-vs-production comparisons, and canary deployment. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.4.1**, **§5.4.4**, **§5.6**) | **Aligned.** Shadow and canary controls are strong evidence of deployment-context validation. |
| **Safety, robustness, and failure response metrics** | NIST expects safety risk evaluation, including robustness, real-time monitoring, and response times for AI system failures. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 2.6**) | SOP includes robustness testing, adversarial perturbation testing for Tier 1 models, rollback triggers, P1/P2 response timelines, and MTTD/MTTR KPIs. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.4.2**, **§5.7.1–§5.7.2**, **§7.1**) | **Aligned.** Response-time and fail-safe mechanisms are defined. |
| **Fairness and bias drift** | NIST requires fairness and bias to be evaluated and documented. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 2.11**) | SOP requires fairness pre-screening, subgroup performance non-regression, demographic parity, equalized odds, disparate impact, counterfactual fairness for Tier 1, and a Fairness Assessment Report. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.2.2**, **§5.4.1**, **§5.4.3**) | **Aligned.** The SOP addresses fairness degradation during retraining. |
| **Independent assessment** | NIST expects internal experts independent from front-line developers and/or independent assessors to be involved in regular assessments. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 1.3**) | SOP assigns Model Validation accountability for validation testing and states Model Validation personnel are independent from development teams. (SOP-AIML-007, **§3**, **§5.5**, **§6.2.3**) | **Aligned.** Independent validation is embedded in the gate. |
| **Risk treatment and prioritization** | NIST MANAGE requires allocating risk resources to mapped/measured risks, prioritizing risks, and establishing plans to respond, recover, and communicate about incidents or events. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **§5.4 MANAGE**) | SOP prioritizes drift tickets P1–P4, sets acknowledgement/resolution timelines, requires validation gates, supports rollback, and defines escalation paths. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.1.2**, **§5.5**, **§5.7**, **§8.3**) | **Aligned.** Risk treatment is prioritized by model tier and severity. |
| **Recovery, rollback, and deactivation-type controls** | NIST MANAGE emphasizes response and recovery plans and continued application of risk management to deployed systems as methods, contexts, risks, and stakeholder expectations evolve. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **§5.4 MANAGE**) | SOP maintains deployable rollback targets, defines rollback triggers, requires RCA, quarantines failed versions, and requires a new validation gate before re-promotion. (SOP-AIML-007, **§4.1 PS-003**, **§5.7.1–§5.7.3**) | **Aligned.** Recovery controls are specific and auditable. |
| **Continual improvement** | NIST states that MANAGE includes mechanisms for continual improvement and ongoing management of deployed AI systems. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **§5.4 MANAGE**) | SOP requires quarterly AI Governance reporting, monthly model risk dashboards, post-rollback RCA reviews, and revision history based on production telemetry and incident postmortems. (SOP-AIML-007, **§7.3**, **§5.7.2**, **§11**) | **Mostly aligned.** Continual improvement exists, but stakeholder feedback loops are underdeveloped. |
| **User and affected-community feedback** | NIST expects feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes, integrated into evaluation metrics. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 3.3**) | SOP allows manual retraining triggers only by model owners, business owners, or Model Validation, and its reports are primarily internal governance reports. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.1.4**, **§7.3**) | **Gap.** The SOP does not define end-user or affected-community reporting, appeals, or integration of such feedback into measurement metrics. |
| **External/emergent risk intelligence** | NIST emphasizes assessing and tracking emergent risks and continuing to apply MANAGE as risks and expectations evolve. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 3.1**, **§5.4 MANAGE**) | SOP includes regulatory/policy-change triggers, adverse-event investigations, audit findings, security vulnerability triggers, and governance reports. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.1.4**, **§5.7.1**, **§7.3**) | **Partial.** The SOP covers internal and regulatory triggers, but does not explicitly require monitoring external AI incident databases, public adverse-event sources, customer complaints, patient/provider feedback, or community impact signals. |

## Key gaps to close

1. **Add an end-user and affected-community feedback channel.**  
   NIST expects problem-reporting and appeal processes from end users and impacted communities to be integrated into AI system evaluation metrics. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 3.3**) SOP-AIML-007 should add intake sources such as clinician reports, patient/provider complaints, customer disputes, appeal outcomes, and community-impact reports, and should connect them to drift/risk dashboards. (SOP-AIML-007, current **§5.1.4**, **§7.2–§7.3**)

2. **Define emergent-risk intelligence sources.**  
   NIST expects regular tracking of existing, unanticipated, and emergent risks. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MEASURE 3.1**) SOP-AIML-007 should explicitly require monitoring external sources such as AI incident databases, regulator safety communications, product complaints, adverse-event databases, cybersecurity advisories, and sector-specific clinical or financial risk signals. (SOP-AIML-007, current **§5.1.4**, **§7.3**)

3. **Tie stakeholder feedback to retraining and rollback triggers.**  
   NIST MANAGE expects risk treatment plans to respond, recover, and communicate about incidents or events. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **§5.4 MANAGE**) SOP-AIML-007 should make certain classes of stakeholder-reported harm, appeals, or adverse outcomes explicit retraining, suspension, rollback, or escalation triggers. (SOP-AIML-007, current **§5.1.2–§5.1.4**, **§5.7.1**, **§8.3**)

4. **Add communication requirements for affected parties.**  
   NIST MANAGE includes communication about incidents or events as part of risk treatment. (NIST AI RMF 1.0, **§5.4 MANAGE**) SOP-AIML-007 currently notifies internal model stakeholders after promotion and reports internally through governance channels, but it does not define when or how impacted users, customers, patients, providers, or affected communities are informed of material model incidents. (SOP-AIML-007, **§5.6**, **§7.3**)

## Overall conclusion

SOP-AIML-007 is **strong for technical distributional drift management**: it defines metrics, thresholds, monitoring cadence, retraining triggers, validation gates, shadow/canary testing, rollback, RCA, and governance reporting. That aligns well with NIST AI RMF **MEASURE 1, MEASURE 2, MEASURE 3.1, and MANAGE §5.4**.

However, it is **not fully aligned for emergent risks** because NIST expects broader feedback and risk-discovery mechanisms involving end users, impacted communities, and evolving deployment context, while the SOP relies mainly on internal monitoring, internal governance, regulatory changes, audits, and adverse-event investigations. The SOP should be updated to include stakeholder feedback, appeals, external incident intelligence, and affected-party communications.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Does SOP-AIML-019 (A/B Testing and Canary Releases for Models) satisfy NIST AI RMF's MANAGE function for production model changes?
question.expected_answer: Partial. The SOP implements canary releases and A/B testing infrastructure that supports gradual rollout — aligning with MANAGE 1 (risk-tier-driven prioritisation) and MANAGE 2 (risk response planning). However, MANAGE 4 specific mitigation procedures are described only at a high level — no explicit halt criteria tied to MEASURE outputs, no defined rollback thresholds for each trustworthiness characteristic, and stakeholder engagement during canaries is mentioned but lacks structured feedback mechanisms (no defined channels, cadence, or escalation path).
question.notes: Partial case grounded in matrix weaknesses.

output.answer:
Yes — **SOP-AIML-019 largely satisfies the NIST AI RMF MANAGE function for controlled production model changes**, but **not fully**. It is strong for A/B/canary change control, go/no-go decisions, rollback, guardrails, monitoring during release, and accountability. The main gaps are **explicit residual-risk documentation, third-party/pre-trained model risk handling, user/affected-community feedback and appeal/override mechanisms, and external incident/error communications**.

| NIST AI RMF MANAGE requirement | SOP-AIML-019 assessment |
|---|---|
| **MANAGE 1.1 — determine whether the AI system achieves intended purposes and whether development/deployment should proceed** | **Satisfied.** SOP-AIML-019 requires an Experiment Design Document with hypothesis, variants, primary success metric, guardrails, sizing/duration, safety/ethical assessment, and rollback criteria before production traffic is routed. It also requires DSRB review, final statistical analysis, DSRB recommendation, and CAIO/CSO go/no-go approval before full rollout. This aligns with NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 1.1**, which requires determining whether the AI system achieves intended purposes and whether deployment should proceed. |
| **MANAGE 1.2 — prioritize treatment of documented AI risks based on impact, likelihood, and resources/methods** | **Partially satisfied.** The SOP prioritizes high-risk clinical and financial models through mandatory guardrails, CSO/financial safety review, safety thresholds, and automatic pauses. However, it does **not explicitly require a documented risk-prioritization method using impact, likelihood, and available resources/methods**, which NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 1.2**, calls for. |
| **MANAGE 1.3 — develop, plan, and document responses to high-priority risks** | **Mostly satisfied.** The SOP documents guardrail breach procedures, automatic pause, RCA within 48 business hours, DSRB/CSO approval before resumption, standard rollback, catastrophic rollback, kill switch, and SEV1 escalation. These support NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 1.3**, which expects planned and documented responses to high-priority AI risks. The weakness is that the SOP does not explicitly frame responses as risk treatment options such as mitigate, transfer, avoid, or accept. |
| **MANAGE 1.4 — document negative residual risks** | **Gap.** The SOP requires final results, practical significance assessment, guardrail status, and rollout approval, but it does **not require explicit documentation of residual risks remaining after rollout**. NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 1.4**, specifically requires documenting negative residual risks to downstream acquirers and end users. |
| **MANAGE 2.1 — account for resources and viable non-AI alternatives to reduce impact/likelihood** | **Gap / weak partial.** The SOP includes roles, approvals, monitoring resources, and technical controls, but it does **not require consideration of non-AI alternatives or resource tradeoffs** as part of the production change decision. NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 2.1**, requires resources and viable non-AI alternatives to be considered. |
| **MANAGE 2.2 — sustain the value of deployed AI systems** | **Partially satisfied.** The SOP supports sustained value through statistically rigorous experiments, practical significance review, false-discovery-rate KPI, monthly experimentation health reporting, and handoff to SOP-AIML-022 for post-rollout monitoring. This aligns with NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 2.2**, which requires mechanisms to sustain value of deployed AI systems. However, because post-deployment monitoring is expressly out of scope and delegated to SOP-AIML-022, SOP-AIML-019 alone is not complete for the full deployed lifecycle. |
| **MANAGE 2.3 — respond to and recover from previously unknown risks** | **Satisfied for production-change context.** The SOP requires automated pause on guardrail breach, immediate CSO notification for high-risk models, RCA within 48 business hours, approval before resumption, rollback, kill switch, and emergency rollback escalation. This aligns with NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 2.3**, which requires procedures to respond to and recover from previously unknown risks. |
| **MANAGE 2.4 — supersede, disengage, or deactivate systems inconsistent with intended use** | **Satisfied.** The SOP includes automatic rollback, treatment traffic set to 0%, zero-traffic kill switch, latency circuit breaker, rollback duration targets, and emergency network isolation if rollback fails. This aligns with NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 2.4**, which requires mechanisms and assigned responsibilities to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that perform inconsistently with intended use. |
| **MANAGE 3.1 / 3.2 — manage third-party resources and pre-trained models** | **Gap if third-party or pre-trained models are involved.** The SOP applies to vendors generally and requires container vulnerability scanning, but it does not define controls for third-party AI resource monitoring, third-party model risk controls, or monitoring of pre-trained models as part of regular maintenance. NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 3.1**, requires third-party AI risks and benefits to be regularly monitored with controls documented, and **MANAGE 3.2** requires pre-trained models used for development to be monitored as part of regular monitoring and maintenance. |
| **MANAGE 4.1 — implement post-deployment monitoring plans, including user input, appeal/override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management** | **Partially satisfied.** The SOP is strong on change management, live experiment monitoring, incident response, recovery, rollback, and deactivation during A/B/canary release. However, it does not itself implement full post-deployment monitoring, user input capture, appeal/override, or decommissioning; it delegates fully rolled-out monitoring to SOP-AIML-022. NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 4.1**, requires post-deployment monitoring plans with those mechanisms. |
| **MANAGE 4.2 — integrate measurable continual improvement activities into AI updates with engagement from relevant AI actors** | **Partially satisfied.** The SOP includes experiment KPIs, monthly health reports, quarterly governance review for high-risk clinical models, DSRB review, CSO review, and revision history. This supports NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 4.2**, which expects measurable continual improvement integrated into updates. The gap is that engagement is mostly internal; the SOP does not clearly require engagement with external interested parties, end users, or affected communities. |
| **MANAGE 4.3 — communicate incidents and errors to relevant AI actors, including affected communities; track, respond, and recover** | **Partially satisfied.** The SOP tracks guardrail breaches, RCA, rollback events, audit logs, Slack alerts, incident tickets, and SEV1 escalation. However, it does not require communication to affected communities, end users, downstream customers, or regulators where applicable. NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 4.3**, requires incidents and errors to be communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities, and for tracking, response, and recovery processes to be followed and documented. |

## Bottom line

**SOP-AIML-019 is a strong production model change-control SOP under the NIST AI RMF MANAGE function**, especially for:

- production A/B testing and canary releases;
- go/no-go decisioning;
- statistical and safety guardrails;
- rollback and deactivation;
- change auditability;
- role-based accountability; and
- incident response during experimentation.

However, to fully satisfy NIST AI RMF MANAGE, it should be updated to add:

1. **Residual risk documentation** before rollout approval, mapped to NIST AI RMF 1.0, **MANAGE 1.4**.  
2. **Formal risk prioritization using impact, likelihood, and resource constraints**, mapped to **MANAGE 1.2**.  
3. **Explicit risk treatment classification** — mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept — mapped to **MANAGE 1.3**.  
4. **Consideration of non-AI alternatives and risk-management resources**, mapped to **MANAGE 2.1**.  
5. **Third-party and pre-trained model risk controls**, mapped to **MANAGE 3.1–3.2**.  
6. **User/affected-community feedback, appeal/override, and decommissioning procedures**, mapped to **MANAGE 4.1**.  
7. **External incident/error communication requirements**, including affected users, customers, communities, and regulators where applicable, mapped to **MANAGE 4.3**.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Is SOP-ITOP-005 (Capacity Planning and Management) compliant with SOC 2's incident-response and change-management expectations?
question.expected_answer: Partial. The capacity-planning programme covers forecasting, monitoring, and scaling actions, but two gaps remain: (1) the incident-response plan exists but tabletop exercises and scenario testing are not on a defined schedule (CC7.4/7.5 expects periodic testing), and (2) capacity-related change procedures lack segregation of duties between approver and implementer (CC8.1). Both are operational specificity gaps rather than missing controls.

output.answer:
Short answer: **partially compliant**. SOP-ITOP-005 is strong for capacity-driven monitoring, escalation, post-incident review, and controlled infrastructure scaling, but it has **material gaps against SOC 2 incident-response testing/effectiveness evaluation** and some **change-management design gaps** for emergency and horizontal capacity changes.

| Area | SOC 2 expectation | SOP-ITOP-005 assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Incident detection and escalation | SOC 2 requires monitoring system components for anomalies and analyzing them to determine whether they represent security events. **SOC 2 CC7.2**. | **Largely meets for capacity events.** The SOP defines continuous Datadog monitoring, Tier 1–3 thresholds, automated ServiceNow incidents, PagerDuty escalation, synthetic checks, and Kafka lag incident triggers. See SOP §§4.2, 5.2. |
| Incident response execution | SOC 2 expects a defined incident-response program with assigned responsibilities, containment/response, mitigation, resolution, restoration, communications, severity assessment, remediation documentation, and communication of remediation activities. **SOC 2 CC7.4**. | **Partially meets.** The SOP assigns roles and provides escalation paths and capacity runbooks; it requires capacity-related SLO breaches to be declared incidents and managed under SOP-ISEC-002, with root cause documented by the Incident Commander. See SOP §§3, 4.5, 5.2, 5.4, 5.5. However, this SOP itself does not define full security-incident communication protocols, containment strategy, or restoration procedures; it relies on SOP-ISEC-002. That reliance is acceptable only if SOP-ISEC-002 contains those controls and is operating effectively. |
| Incident response testing and effectiveness | SOC 2 expects incident-response activities to be evaluated for effectiveness periodically. **SOC 2 CC7.4**. SOC 2 also expects periodic incident-recovery plan testing with scenarios based on threat likelihood and magnitude, relevant system components, key-personnel unavailability, and plan revisions based on results. **SOC 2 CC7.4, continued**. | **Gap.** SOP §4.5 explicitly states that tabletop exercises to rehearse response procedures are “not currently scheduled.” That conflicts with SOC 2’s expectation for periodic evaluation/testing of incident response and recovery. Post-incident reviews in SOP §5.5 help with lessons learned, but they do not substitute for periodic planned testing. |
| Lessons learned and recurrence prevention | SOC 2 expects lessons learned to improve response and recovery procedures and changes to prevent/detect recurrences. **SOC 2 CC7.4, continued**. | **Mostly meets.** SOP §5.5 requires a post-incident review within 5 business days for P1/P2 capacity incidents and creates Jira action items for baseline, alerting, and runbook improvements. This aligns well with recurrence-prevention expectations. |
| Change authorization and approval | SOC 2 requires changes to infrastructure, data, software, and procedures to be authorized, documented, tracked, tested, approved, and implemented to meet objectives. **SOC 2 CC8.1**. | **Mostly meets, with inconsistency.** SOP §4.4 requires production capacity changes to be authorized through a ServiceNow Change Request and approved under SOP-CHG-001 with segregation of duties. SOP §§5.4.1–5.4.2 require Git branches, PRs, plan/diff outputs, peer/director approval, and post-change validation. However, the horizontal scaling runbook in SOP §5.4.1 does not explicitly include creating or linking a ServiceNow Change Request, even though SOP §4.4 says all such production capacity changes must have one. |
| Change testing before production | SOC 2 expects system changes to be tested before implementation into production. **SOC 2 CC8.1**. | **Partial.** SOP §5.4.1 uses `terraform plan` or `helm diff`, and SOP §5.4.2 requires PR/change review, but the SOP does not clearly require pre-production testing, automated validation, canary deployment, or rollback testing before production scaling changes. Post-deployment validation in SOP §5.4.1 is useful, but SOC 2 CC8.1 specifically points to testing prior to production implementation. |
| Segregation of duties | SOC 2 expects deployment of changes with consideration of segregation of responsibilities to prevent or detect unauthorized changes. **SOC 2 CC8.1**. | **Meets.** SOP §4.4 prohibits the same person from implementing and approving a production capacity change. SOP §6.2 enforces branch protection, CODEOWNERS review, restricted approvals, and ServiceNow implementer/approver separation. |
| Emergency changes | SOC 2 expects a process for authorizing, designing, testing, approving, and implementing emergency changes in urgent time frames. **SOC 2 CC8.1**. | **Partial.** SOP §§8.2–8.3 define exception and escalation processes, and SOP §6.1 defines break-glass logging for manual changes. However, the SOP does not clearly define emergency-change requirements for capacity scaling, such as minimum emergency approval, retrospective change record timing, testing expectations, rollback requirements, and post-emergency review linkage. |
| Capacity-driven change management | SOC 2 Availability requires current capacity monitoring, baseline usage measurement, forecasting of average/peak use, and initiating change management when forecasted usage exceeds tolerances. **SOC 2 A1.1**. | **Strongly meets.** SOP §§5.1–5.3 define baselines, continuous monitoring, threshold tiers, quarterly forecasting, forecast reports, and capacity-driven changes. SOP §4.4 requires capacity-altering production changes to follow change management. |

## Required remediation

1. **Schedule periodic incident-response and recovery testing.** Add at least annual tabletop exercises and technical recovery simulations for capacity-related outages and capacity-driven security events, with scenarios covering key-personnel unavailability and system-component failure. This is needed for **SOC 2 CC7.4**.

2. **Make horizontal scaling explicitly create or link a ServiceNow Change Request.** SOP §5.4.1 should mirror SOP §4.4 by requiring a CHG record for both forecast-driven and incident-driven horizontal scaling, or clearly document when an emergency change process applies. This supports **SOC 2 CC8.1**.

3. **Add pre-production/change testing requirements.** Define what counts as acceptable testing for capacity changes: Terraform/Helm validation, CI checks, staging test, canary deployment, load test where applicable, and rollback verification. This supports **SOC 2 CC8.1**.

4. **Define emergency change handling more explicitly.** Include minimum approval, emergency implementation authority, required retrospective review/approval, ServiceNow record timing, rollback plan, and post-emergency PIR. This supports **SOC 2 CC8.1**.

5. **Confirm dependency on SOP-ISEC-002.** Because SOP-ITOP-005 delegates incident handling to SOP-ISEC-002, Meridian should ensure SOP-ISEC-002 covers SOC 2 CC7.4 elements including containment, remediation, restoration, stakeholder communications, and periodic effectiveness testing.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Is SOP-LEGC-001 (Regulatory Change Management) compliant with GDPR's transparency and international-transfer requirements?
question.expected_answer: Partial. The SOP acknowledges international transfers and tracks GDPR developments, but two gaps remain: (1) Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) and transfer-impact-assessment procedures are not explicitly referenced as the operational mechanism under Chapter V; and (2) the privacy-notice update workflow tied to regulatory change exists but does not enumerate the Articles 13/14 elements that must be reflected (purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention, rights, transfers). Direction is right; operational specifics are missing.

output.answer:
No. **SOP-LEGC-001 is only partially compliant** with GDPR transparency and international-transfer requirements. It provides a reasonable **governance/change-management framework** for detecting and remediating GDPR changes, but it does **not contain the substantive operating procedures or controls needed to satisfy GDPR Articles 12–15 and Chapter V transfers.**

## Assessment summary

| Area | GDPR requirement | SOP evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regulatory-change governance | Controllers must implement and update appropriate technical/organizational measures and be able to demonstrate GDPR compliance. | SOP §§1.1, 4, 5.1–5.4 create horizon scanning, impact assessment, remediation, control validation, and audit trail. | **Mostly aligned** with GDPR accountability expectations. |
| Transparency notices | Information must be provided in concise, transparent, intelligible, easily accessible form; privacy information must include controller/DPO details, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, rights, complaint rights, automated decision-making, and transfer details where applicable. | SOP mentions GDPR in scope and DPO consultation, but does not define privacy notice content, ownership, review triggers, publication channels, or timing. | **Gap** |
| Data subject communications | Controllers must facilitate rights and respond without undue delay and within one month, with extension rules. | SOP does not define DSAR/rights-response procedures or how regulatory changes update data-subject communications. | **Gap** |
| International-transfer mechanism | Transfers to third countries/international organizations must comply with GDPR Chapter V and not undermine GDPR protection. | SOP has generic data-lineage and data-locality controls, e.g., “EU data stays in AWS Frankfurt,” but lacks a transfer-mechanism decision process. | **Gap** |
| Appropriate safeguards and data-subject rights | In absence of adequacy, transfers require appropriate safeguards and enforceable rights/effective remedies, e.g., SCCs, BCRs, approved codes/certifications. | SOP does not require identifying adequacy decisions, SCCs/BCRs, derogations, onward-transfer controls, or evidence of safeguards. | **Gap** |
| DPO involvement | DPO tasks include informing/advising, monitoring compliance, advising on DPIAs, cooperating with supervisory authorities. | SOP §3 makes the DPO “Consulted and informed on all RCIs impacting personal data.” | **Partially aligned**, but DPO involvement is not tied to privacy notices or transfer approvals. |

## Detailed findings

### 1. The SOP has a sound GDPR governance backbone

SOP-LEGC-001 establishes a controlled regulatory-change process: horizon scanning, applicability assessment, gap analysis, remediation planning, validation, and closure evidence under SOP §§5.1–5.4. That supports GDPR’s accountability model because GDPR requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and be able to demonstrate that processing is performed in accordance with the Regulation, with measures reviewed and updated where necessary. **GDPR Article 24(1)–(2).**

The SOP also requires traceability from regulatory obligation to implemented control under SOP §4, POL-LEGC-001-C, which aligns with GDPR’s accountability principle that controllers are responsible for and must be able to demonstrate compliance with the GDPR principles. **GDPR Article 5(2).**

### 2. Transparency requirements are not operationalized

GDPR transparency is not just a change-management requirement. Controllers must provide information to data subjects in a “concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form,” using clear and plain language. **GDPR Article 12(1).** Controllers must also facilitate data-subject rights and respond to rights requests without undue delay and in any event within one month, subject to limited extension rules. **GDPR Article 12(2)–(4).**

For data collected directly from the data subject, required notice content includes controller identity, DPO contact details, purposes and legal basis, legitimate interests where applicable, recipients, transfer details and safeguards, retention, data-subject rights, withdrawal of consent, complaint rights, statutory/contractual necessity, and automated decision-making information. **GDPR Article 13(1)–(3).** For data not obtained from the data subject, similar information is required, including categories of data, source, transfer information, safeguards, and timing rules. **GDPR Article 14(1)–(3).**

SOP-LEGC-001 does **not** include a privacy-notice procedure that specifies:

- who owns privacy notice drafting, approval, publication, and versioning;
- required GDPR Article 13/14 content;
- notice timing rules for direct and indirect collection;
- rules for notifying data subjects of new processing purposes before further processing;
- requirements for clear and plain language;
- how automated decision-making/profiling disclosures are reviewed;
- how international-transfer disclosures are incorporated into notices.

The SOP’s Revision History says version 2.7 “Updated international data transfer procedures and privacy notice requirements,” but the operative sections do not actually contain those procedures. A revision-history statement is not an enforceable control.

### 3. Data-subject access transparency is missing

GDPR gives data subjects the right to access information about processing, including purposes, categories, recipients, retention, rights, complaint rights, source of data, automated decision-making, and recipients in third countries or international organizations. **GDPR Article 15(1).** Where personal data are transferred to a third country or international organization, the data subject has the right to be informed of the appropriate safeguards under Article 46. **GDPR Article 15(2).**

SOP-LEGC-001 does not define how regulatory changes affecting Article 15 access disclosures are implemented, tested, or validated. The generic RCI process could capture such a change, but the SOP does not require the resulting control to update DSAR response templates, data maps used for access responses, or transfer-safeguard disclosures.

### 4. International-transfer controls are materially incomplete

GDPR Chapter V requires that any transfer of personal data to a third country or international organization occur only if Chapter V conditions are met, including onward transfers, and that GDPR-level protection is not undermined. **GDPR Article 44.**

Transfers may rely on an adequacy decision. **GDPR Article 45.** In the absence of adequacy, transfers require appropriate safeguards and enforceable data-subject rights/effective legal remedies, such as standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, approved codes of conduct, or certification mechanisms. **GDPR Article 46(1)–(2).** Derogations are limited to specific situations such as explicit informed consent, contractual necessity, important public interest, legal claims, vital interests, or limited non-repetitive compelling legitimate interests with additional safeguards and supervisory-authority/data-subject notification where applicable. **GDPR Article 49(1).** Foreign court or administrative orders requiring disclosure are only recognized/enforceable if based on an international agreement, without prejudice to other Chapter V transfer grounds. **GDPR Article 48.**

SOP-LEGC-001 contains helpful adjacent controls, including:

- data lineage as a prerequisite for obligations concerning data rights, use limitation, or data quality, SOP §4, POL-LEGC-001-B;
- data-lineage documentation in Alation, SOP §5.3.3;
- vendor regulatory review for high-risk vendors, SOP §6.1 AC-04;
- a data-locality example: “EU data stays in AWS Frankfurt,” SOP §6.2 TC-02.

However, these are insufficient for Chapter V compliance. The SOP does **not** require:

- a transfer inventory identifying third-country recipients and onward transfers;
- mapping each transfer to an Article 45 adequacy decision, Article 46 safeguard, or Article 49 derogation;
- SCC/BCR/code/certification selection and approval workflow;
- evidence that enforceable data-subject rights and effective remedies are available;
- assessment and approval of transfer-risk/safeguard changes;
- controls for foreign-government access requests under Article 48;
- procedures to update privacy notices and access-response disclosures with transfer safeguards under Articles 13, 14, and 15.

### 5. DPO role is present but too weak for these requirements

SOP §3 states the DPO is consulted and informed on all RCIs impacting personal data. That is directionally consistent with GDPR Article 39, which assigns the DPO tasks to inform and advise the controller or processor, monitor compliance, advise on DPIAs, cooperate with the supervisory authority, and act as a supervisory-authority contact point. **GDPR Article 39(1).**

But for transparency and international transfers, the SOP should require DPO review/approval for privacy notice changes, transfer-mechanism selection, high-risk transfer escalations, and supervisory-authority/data-subject communications where Article 49 or Article 48 issues arise. The current “consulted and informed” wording is not enough to show operational compliance.

## Required remediation

To make SOP-LEGC-001 compliant for GDPR transparency and international transfers, add explicit GDPR workstreams or appendices covering:

1. **Privacy Notice Change Control**
   - Required Article 13/14 content checklist.
   - Plain-language and accessibility review under Article 12.
   - Trigger for privacy notice updates when purposes, recipients, legal bases, automated decision-making, retention, or transfers change.
   - DPO/legal approval and publication/versioning requirements.

2. **Data Subject Rights Communications**
   - Link RCI changes to DSAR/access-response templates.
   - Require Article 15 transfer-safeguard disclosures where third-country transfers exist.
   - Include Article 12 timing and extension controls.

3. **International Transfer Assessment**
   - Transfer inventory and lineage to third-country recipients.
   - Decision tree: Article 45 adequacy → Article 46 safeguards → Article 49 derogation only if necessary.
   - Required evidence for SCCs, BCRs, codes, certifications, or derogations.
   - Onward-transfer review.
   - DPO/legal approval before transfer go-live.

4. **Article 48 Government-Access Procedure**
   - Escalation path for foreign court/authority requests.
   - Legal review for international agreement basis or other Chapter V ground.

5. **Control Validation Evidence**
   - Privacy notice screenshot/version history.
   - Transfer-mechanism approval record.
   - Executed SCC/BCR or adequacy reference.
   - Updated ROPA/data map/lineage.
   - DSAR template update evidence.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Does SOP-AIML-006 (Model Performance Monitoring) satisfy NIST AI RMF's expectations for ongoing risk measurement and management?
question.expected_answer: Partial. Performance monitoring covers MEASURE 2 (continuous tracking of identified risks) reasonably well, but: (1) MANAGE function is described at a high level — no specific mitigation procedures tied to particular MEASURE outputs and threshold breaches; (2) Stakeholder engagement is mentioned but lacks structured feedback mechanisms (no defined cadence, channel, or escalation owner). The skeleton is correct; operationalisation is incomplete.

output.answer:
## Short answer

SOP-AIML-006 **partially satisfies** NIST AI RMF expectations for ongoing risk measurement and management. It is strong on **post-deployment technical performance monitoring, drift detection, alerting, rollback/fallback response, escalation, and reporting**, which aligns well with NIST AI RMF’s **MEASURE** and parts of **MANAGE** functions. However, it does **not fully satisfy** NIST AI RMF because it is primarily a model-performance/operations SOP and does not sufficiently cover the broader AI-risk expectations around **risk tolerance, full trustworthiness characteristics, stakeholder/affected-community feedback, independent assessment, residual-risk documentation, and enterprise risk integration**.

## Where SOP-AIML-006 aligns with NIST AI RMF

| NIST AI RMF expectation | SOP-AIML-006 evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Ongoing production monitoring of AI system behavior | The SOP requires continuous monitoring of production and shadow-mode models, including data drift, prediction drift, performance metrics, latency, traffic, and dashboards in Arize. (SOP-AIML-006 §§1.1, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4) NIST expects AI system functionality and behavior to be monitored in production. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.3, Table 3, MEASURE 2.4) | **Meets** for technical performance monitoring. |
| Use of appropriate metrics and documentation of measurement methods | The SOP defines model-specific metrics such as AUROC, sensitivity, specificity, F1, RMSE, ROUGE-L, hallucination rate, PSI, and latency, and requires baseline metric capture and dashboard configuration. (SOP-AIML-006 §§5.1, 5.2, 5.3) NIST expects appropriate methods and metrics for AI-risk measurement to be selected and applied, and TEVV test sets, metrics, and tools to be documented. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.3, Table 3, MEASURE 1.1 and MEASURE 2.1) | **Substantially meets** for model-performance risk. |
| Deployment-context measurement | The SOP uses sliding windows, ground-truth pipelines, delayed-label handling, clinical/financial/operational model categories, and production dashboards. (SOP-AIML-006 §§1.2, 5.2.2, 6.2) NIST expects performance or assurance criteria to be measured under conditions similar to deployment settings. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.3, Table 3, MEASURE 2.3) | **Meets** for deployment performance. |
| Regular reassessment and updates | The SOP requires ongoing KPI reviews, weekly/monthly/quarterly reporting, quarterly failure-injection drills, post-mortems, and exception handling. (SOP-AIML-006 §§7.1, 7.2, 8.1, 9.1) NIST expects metric appropriateness and existing control effectiveness to be regularly assessed and updated. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.3, Table 3, MEASURE 1.2) | **Partially meets**; reviews exist, but the SOP does not require broader reassessment of AI-risk metrics beyond monitoring-program KPIs and performance thresholds. |
| Risk response, recovery, and communication | The SOP defines Critical alert triage, incident declaration, stakeholder notification, rollback, traffic shunting, feature-off fallback, RCA, post-mortems, and unresolved-degradation escalation. (SOP-AIML-006 §§5.5, 6.1, 8.2) NIST states that the MANAGE function includes plans to respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.4) | **Meets** for operational degradation incidents. |
| Deactivation or disengagement of underperforming systems | The SOP allows rollback, fallback, feature-flag shutoff, and formal remediation-or-sunset review when degradation remains unresolved for more than seven days. (SOP-AIML-006 §§5.5, 8.2) NIST expects mechanisms to manage risks of deployed systems and improve or disengage systems as risks evolve over time. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.4; see also NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.1, GOVERN 1.7 on safe decommissioning) | **Mostly meets**, though decommissioning is addressed procedurally only for unresolved performance degradation. |

## Key gaps against NIST AI RMF

1. **Risk measurement is too narrow.**  
   SOP-AIML-006 focuses on performance, drift, latency, traffic, infrastructure health, and ground-truth validation. (SOP-AIML-006 §§5.2–5.4, 6.2, 6.3) NIST AI RMF expects AI systems to be evaluated across trustworthy characteristics, including validity and reliability, safety, security and resilience, accountability and transparency, explainability and interpretability, privacy enhancement, and fairness with harmful bias managed. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3; §5.3, Table 3, MEASURE 2) The SOP does not define ongoing monitoring metrics for fairness, bias, privacy impacts, safety harms, explainability quality, user overreliance, or downstream human-impact risk.

2. **No explicit risk-tolerance framework.**  
   The SOP defines alert thresholds for metrics such as AUROC, F1, PSI, latency, and missing feature rate. (SOP-AIML-006 §5.4.1) NIST states that organizations should define risk tolerance, that tolerance is contextual and use-case specific, and that risk management should document processes once tolerance is defined. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §1.2.2) The SOP’s thresholds are operational thresholds, but it does not tie them to documented AI-risk tolerances, harm severity, affected populations, clinical or financial impact, or residual-risk acceptance criteria.

3. **Limited stakeholder and affected-community feedback.**  
   The SOP includes internal stakeholders such as Model Owners, MLOps, AI/ML Engineering, Product Managers, executives, and auditors. (SOP-AIML-006 §§5.5, 7.2, 9) NIST expects measurement results and performance changes to be informed by domain experts, relevant AI actors, end users, and, where appropriate, affected communities. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.3, Table 3, MEASURE 1.3, MEASURE 4.2, MEASURE 4.3) The SOP does not require collecting user, patient, customer, clinician, member, or affected-community feedback as part of ongoing risk measurement.

4. **No end-user problem-reporting or appeal integration.**  
   The SOP uses PagerDuty, ServiceNow, Slack, Arize, RCA, and post-mortems for internal operational incident handling. (SOP-AIML-006 §§5.4, 5.5, 8.1) NIST expects feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes to be established and integrated into AI-system evaluation metrics. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.3, Table 3, MEASURE 3.3) SOP-AIML-006 does not include an external complaint, appeal, patient-safety event, adverse-outcome, or customer-impact feedback loop.

5. **Independent assessment is not clearly required.**  
   The SOP requires Model Owners and MLOps teams to perform monitoring, response, RCA, reporting, and drills. (SOP-AIML-006 §§5.2, 5.5, 7.2, 9.1) NIST expects internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers and/or independent assessors to be involved in regular assessments and updates. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.3, Table 3, MEASURE 1.3) The SOP includes auditors in training, but it does not require independent periodic review of monitoring thresholds, incidents, metric appropriateness, or risk decisions. (SOP-AIML-006 §9)

6. **Risk management is not clearly integrated with enterprise risk management.**  
   The SOP includes executive quarterly summaries and regulatory posture reporting. (SOP-AIML-006 §7.2) NIST states that AI risk management should be integrated into broader enterprise risk management strategies and processes. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §1.2.4) The SOP does not specify linkage to an enterprise risk register, risk owners outside engineering, residual-risk acceptance, CAPA governance triggers beyond references, or formal executive risk acceptance.

7. **Residual risk and risk-treatment decisions are underdeveloped.**  
   The SOP has exception requests, incident response, rollback, fallback, and sunset review. (SOP-AIML-006 §§5.5, 8.1, 8.2) NIST expects ongoing management of deployed AI systems as contexts, risks, methods, and stakeholder expectations evolve, and the MANAGE function includes prioritizing risk, regular monitoring, improvement, and risk treatment. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.4) The SOP does not require documenting residual risk after incidents, risk-treatment options considered, rationale for accepting continued operation, or impact/likelihood-based prioritization.

## Overall conclusion

SOP-AIML-006 is a strong **MLOps performance-monitoring control** and would provide meaningful evidence for NIST AI RMF **MEASURE 1.1, MEASURE 1.2, MEASURE 2.1, MEASURE 2.3, MEASURE 2.4**, and portions of **MANAGE** related to response, recovery, escalation, and deactivation. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §5.3, Table 3; §5.4) However, it does not, by itself, fully satisfy NIST AI RMF’s expectations for ongoing AI risk measurement and management because the RMF expects broader socio-technical risk measurement, stakeholder feedback, independent assessment, risk tolerance, residual-risk handling, and enterprise-risk integration. (NIST AI RMF 1.0 §§1.2.2, 1.2.4, 5.3, 5.4)

Recommended remediation: add a section requiring ongoing measurement of fairness, safety, privacy, security/resilience, explainability, human-impact, and adverse-outcome risks; require independent periodic review; integrate end-user/affected-community feedback and appeals; document residual risk and risk acceptance; and connect model monitoring outcomes to the enterprise AI risk register and executive risk-governance process.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Does SOP-FIN-002 (Fraud Detection System Operations) meet SR 11-7's governance and inventory expectations?
question.expected_answer: Partial. SOP-FIN-002 establishes ongoing performance monitoring and validation activities, but two governance pieces are incomplete: (1) the model inventory exists but lacks an explicit risk-tiering methodology mapping fraud models to materiality/impact and validation intensity; (2) the governance structure mentions model owners and validators but does not clearly delineate independence — i.e. who owns vs who challenges, and how reporting lines preserve effective challenge.

expected_citations.section: Section III (Validation), Section V (Governance — inventory + roles)

output.answer:
SOP-FIN-002 **partially meets** SR 11-7 governance and inventory expectations.

### Bottom line

The SOP is strong on **operational governance** for the fraud detection system and provides a meaningful control framework for the ML fraud model, but it does **not fully evidence an SR 11-7-complete model governance and inventory program** within the SOP itself. The biggest gaps are: (1) limited senior management/board-level model risk oversight, (2) insufficient detail on what the enterprise model inventory contains for the HML-FM model, and (3) some ambiguity around independence of model validation.

---

## 1. Applicability under SR 11-7

The **HML-FM ML Fraud Model v3.2** is within SR 11-7’s model-risk scope because SR 11-7 applies to complex quantitative/statistical approaches that process inputs into quantitative estimates; it expressly distinguishes these from simple arithmetic and deterministic rule-based processes. **SR 11-7, Section II / Purpose and Scope; Section III / Overview of Model Risk and Model Risk Management.**

The SOP’s deterministic fraud rules are less clearly “models” for SR 11-7 purposes because the current guidance excludes deterministic rule-based processes where no statistical, economic, or financial theory underpins the design or use. **SR 11-7, Section II / Purpose and Scope.** The SOP’s ML fraud model, however, should be governed as a model.

---

## 2. Governance expectations

SR 11-7 expects model governance to be supported by **clear policies, effective controls, defined risk-management expectations, and a framework for assessing model risk and applying practices commensurate with risk**. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Governance and Controls.**

### What the SOP does well

SOP-FIN-002 includes several governance elements aligned to SR 11-7:

- It establishes a model governance policy for fraud detection models, requiring initial and annual model risk assessments, validation, monitoring, and Model Governance Committee review. **SOP-FIN-002, Section 4.2; SR 11-7, Section VI / Governance and Controls.**
- It defines roles and responsibilities through a RACI matrix covering model retraining, performance monitoring, decommissioning, third-party validation, regulatory reporting, and rule changes. **SOP-FIN-002, Section 3.1; SR 11-7, Section VI / Roles and Responsibilities.**
- It addresses conflicts of interest by prohibiting validation by individuals directly involved in model development during the current validation cycle. **SOP-FIN-002, Section 4.2 and Section 6.3; SR 11-7, Section VI / Roles and Responsibilities.**
- It includes ongoing monitoring through model performance dashboards, drift thresholds, KPIs, quarterly model performance reviews, and retraining triggers. **SOP-FIN-002, Sections 5.2.2, 7.1, 7.2, and 7.3; SR 11-7, Section VI / Governance and Controls.**
- It includes third-party oversight for model validation consultants and external fraud data providers, which supports SR 11-7’s expectation that externally supported model-risk activities remain under proper oversight and integrated into broader model-risk management. **SOP-FIN-002, Section 6.4; SR 11-7, Section VI / Roles and Responsibilities; Section VII / Vendor and Other Third-Party Products.**

### Governance gaps

The SOP does **not fully meet** SR 11-7 governance expectations because:

1. **Board or senior enterprise-level oversight is not clearly defined.**  
   SR 11-7 expects governance to establish accountability and effective controls across the model lifecycle. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Governance and Controls; Section VI / Roles and Responsibilities.** SOP-FIN-002 identifies the VP Financial Services, CFO in revision approval, and the Model Governance Committee, but it does not specify board-level, board committee, or enterprise risk committee oversight for material model risk. **SOP-FIN-002, Sections 3.2, 4.2, and 11.**

2. **Model risk appetite/materiality methodology is not sufficiently described.**  
   SR 11-7 expects policies to establish a framework for assessing the magnitude of model risk and applying model-risk management commensurate with that risk. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Governance and Controls.** The SOP requires annual model risk assessments, but it does not define risk-tiering criteria, materiality factors, or how fraud model risk is aggregated or escalated at the enterprise level. **SOP-FIN-002, Section 4.2.**

3. **Validation independence is directionally addressed but somewhat inconsistent.**  
   SR 11-7 expects clear roles and responsibilities and attention to conflicts of interest between development and validation groups. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Roles and Responsibilities.** The SOP says Fraud Data Science “executes model validation activities” while also stating that validation cannot be performed by individuals directly involved in development and that validation may be performed by the Model Governance Committee or an independent validator. **SOP-FIN-002, Sections 3.2, 4.2, and 6.3.** This should be clarified so validation responsibility is independent from development, not merely separated at the individual level within the same function.

---

## 3. Model inventory expectations

SR 11-7 states that banking organizations commonly maintain a **comprehensive model inventory** with enough information to understand model risks and support model-risk management at both the individual and aggregate levels. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Model Inventory.**

### What the SOP does well

The SOP states that the Model Governance Committee maintains Meridian’s enterprise model inventory and that all active fraud detection models are included. **SOP-FIN-002, Sections 3.2 and 4.2; SR 11-7, Section VI / Model Inventory.**

The SOP also has a strong **fraud rule inventory** for deterministic rules, including rule ID, description, logic, deployment date, version, priority, fraud typology, status, last performance review date, and linked change-request documentation. **SOP-FIN-002, Section 5.1.2.** This is useful operationally, though deterministic rules may not be “models” under SR 11-7 where they lack statistical or quantitative model characteristics. **SR 11-7, Section II / Purpose and Scope.**

### Inventory gaps

The SOP does **not define the required data fields for the model inventory** for HML-FM or other fraud models. SR 11-7 expects inventory information sufficient to understand model risks and manage those risks individually and in aggregate. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Model Inventory.**

At minimum, the SOP should require the model inventory to include:

- Model name, unique model ID, version, and status.
- Business owner, technical owner, developer, validator, and approver.
- Purpose, intended use, actual use, and business line.
- Model type/algorithm, key inputs, outputs, and dependencies.
- Inherent risk rating, materiality, and exposure.
- Limitations, assumptions, known weaknesses, and prohibited uses.
- Validation date, validation conclusion, open findings, remediation status, and next validation due date.
- Monitoring metrics, drift thresholds, performance history, and exception history.
- Implementation date, change history, retirement/decommissioning status.
- Third-party components, data providers, and vendor dependencies, where applicable.

Without these details, the SOP only states that an inventory exists; it does not establish that the inventory is comprehensive enough to support SR 11-7 model-risk management. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Model Inventory.**

---

## Overall assessment

SOP-FIN-002 has a credible governance structure for day-to-day fraud detection and includes many SR 11-7-aligned elements: RACI, model governance committee, model performance monitoring, change control, exception handling, conflict-of-interest controls, training, and third-party oversight. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Governance and Controls; Section VI / Roles and Responsibilities; Section VII / Vendor and Other Third-Party Products.**

However, it falls short of a full SR 11-7 governance and inventory standard because it does not clearly define enterprise-level model risk oversight, does not describe risk-tiering/materiality for model governance, and does not specify required model inventory content sufficient to manage model risk individually and in aggregate. **SR 11-7, Section VI / Governance and Controls; Section VI / Model Inventory.**

Recommended remediation: add a dedicated **SR 11-7 Model Governance and Inventory** subsection defining model risk tiering, senior management/board reporting, validation independence, inventory fields, inventory reconciliation, and escalation of material model-risk issues.

Compliance level: partial

question.question: Is SOP-AIML-006 (Model Performance Monitoring) compliant with SR 11-7's three foundational elements?
question.expected_answer: Gap. Despite addressing monitoring at the technical level, the SOP fails on the governance dimension: no escalation path for model-risk findings to the board/senior management (SR 11-7 Section V), no challenger-model expectation for high-impact decisions (Section III — effective challenge), and no overarching model risk management framework or model inventory tying monitoring back to the bank's model population. These are core SR 11-7 structures and their absence is non-compliance, not partial.

output.answer:
Based on SOP-AIML-006 alone, the SOP is **partially compliant** with SR 11-7’s three foundational model risk management elements. It is strong for **ongoing model performance monitoring**, but it does not fully cover **model development/use**, **independent validation/effective challenge**, or full **governance and controls** expected under SR 11-7.

| SR 11-7 foundational element | Assessment of SOP-AIML-006 | Compliance view |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Model development, implementation, and use** | SR 11-7 expects model development to be aligned with model purpose, business use, and policy, and recognizes that developer judgment affects conceptual design, inputs, and soundness. **SR 11-7 §IV, Model Development and Model Use.** SOP-AIML-006 requires model registry entries, model purpose, owner, training dataset snapshot, dependencies, baseline metrics, baseline data distributions, SLAs, and monitoring dashboard setup. **SOP §§5.1–5.2.** However, SOP-AIML-006 expressly excludes pre-deployment validation and acceptance testing and does not require documentation of conceptual soundness, assumptions, limitations, model design rationale, intended-use limitations, or implementation verification beyond monitoring onboarding. **SOP §1.3; SR 11-7 §IV.** | **Partial** |
| **2. Model validation** | SR 11-7 treats model validation as a core model risk management element and expects effective challenge by objective experts with appropriate expertise, independence, and authority. **SR 11-7 §III, Overview of Model Risk and Model Risk Management; SR 11-7 §V, Model Validation.** SOP-AIML-006 contains meaningful ongoing monitoring controls: drift monitoring, performance metric calculation, delayed-label pipelines, ground-truth validation pipelines, incident RCA, rollback/fallback procedures, and post-mortems. **SOP §§5.2–5.5, 6.1–6.2.** But it does not establish an independent validation function, validation sign-off, periodic revalidation, validation reporting, or independent review of monitoring thresholds and outcomes. It also places response and RCA primarily with the Model Owner and MLOps rather than an independent challenger. **SOP §§5.5, 6.2; SR 11-7 §III and §V.** | **Partial / Gap for independence** |
| **3. Governance, policies, and controls** | SR 11-7 expects model governance to be supported by clear policies and effective controls; procedures should allocate resources and establish monitoring and control processes. **SR 11-7 §VI, Governance and Controls.** SOP-AIML-006 includes defined monitoring procedures, alert thresholds, rollback gates, access control, exception handling, escalation, KPIs, reporting cadence, and training. **SOP §§5–9.** It also supports model inventory through required model registry entries. **SOP §5.1; SR 11-7 §VI, Model Inventory.** However, it does not fully address model risk tiering/materiality, aggregate model risk, conflicts of interest, internal audit oversight, board or risk committee oversight, or formal governance over third-party/vendor model validation. SR 11-7 specifically calls for clear roles and responsibilities, accountability, conflict-of-interest consideration, effective governance, inventory, documentation, and vendor-product validation/monitoring. **SR 11-7 §VI, Governance and Controls; SR 11-7 §VII, Vendor and Other Third-Party Products.** | **Partial** |

### Key strengths

- **Strong ongoing monitoring design:** SOP-AIML-006 defines baseline registration, performance metrics by model type, drift detection, alert thresholds, delayed ground-truth handling, and operational KPIs.
